title: Created in God’s Image
objective: Students will explore how the Harlem Renaissance was a profound affirmation of human dignity rooted in the theological conviction that every person is made *imago Dei* — in the image and likeness of God. They will connect Catholic Social Teaching Principle 1 (Life and Dignity of the Human Person) to the cultural and artistic work of the Renaissance, and reflect on their own responsibility to affirm the dignity of others.
materials: Projected or printed Aaron Douglas image — *Song of the Towers* or *Aspects of Negro Life*
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the exhibition:** Bring your class to experience the phonograph, the Great Migration Map, the Jazz Lab, and more. Ask your librarian to arrange a visit. **Option 2 — Virtual visit:**

steps.title: Two questions
script: *“I’m going to ask you two questions. First: what does it mean to be made in God’s image? Take 30 seconds and write one sentence. Second: if every person is made in God’s image — equally — what does it mean when a society treats some people as less than others?”*
Take 4–5 responses to each. Hold the tension between the theological claim and the historical reality. Don’t resolve it yet.

screen.question: What does it mean to be made in God’s image? If every person is made in God’s image — equally — what does it mean when a society treats some people as less than others?

steps.purpose: Hold the tension between the theological claim and the historical reality. Don’t resolve it yet.
students: Take 30 seconds and write one sentence for each.

steps.title: Imago Dei
script: Establish the theological foundation: *imago Dei* (Genesis 1:26–27) means every human person possesses inherent, irreducible dignity — not earned by achievement, status, race, or talent. This is not a social convention; it is a theological claim about the nature of reality.

verse.text: “Then God said, ‘Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness’... So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them.”

steps.purpose: Establish the theological foundation: dignity is given, not earned.
students: What does this passage say about every person’s value?

steps.title: In paint and poetry and jazz
script: *“The artists, writers, and musicians of the Harlem Renaissance were making exactly this claim — but in paint and poetry and jazz. Langston Hughes was saying: ‘I, too, am America.’ Aaron Douglas was painting figures without individual faces because the point was not one person’s dignity — it was every Black person’s dignity. That is a theological argument expressed in art.”*

steps.purpose: See the claim of *imago Dei* made in art.
students: Langston Hughes was saying: ‘I, too, am America.’
How does this painting affirm the idea of *imago Dei*?

steps.title: Solidarity
script: Introduce the historical context briefly: Jim Crow laws, segregation, and the cultural response of the Harlem Renaissance as an assertion that Black life, art, and culture were not only equal but magnificent. Connect to CST Principle 7 — Solidarity: what happens to one member of the human family affects all of us.

screen.text: What happens to one member of the human family affects all of us.

steps.purpose: Connect the Renaissance’s response to injustice to the call to solidarity.
students: What does solidarity ask of us today?

steps.title: Choose a handout

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read Genesis 1:26–27 and a short summary of CST Principle 1. Answer four guided questions connecting the theological text to the Harlem Renaissance. Draw or describe one moment from the Renaissance that expressed human dignity.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Read two scripture passages and apply CST Principle 1 to two specific examples from the Harlem Renaissance. Write a reflective paragraph on what it means to affirm someone’s *imago Dei* through creative work — and what students’ responsibility is today.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Theological analysis: how does the Harlem Renaissance represent a response to the systematic violation of *imago Dei*? Write a structured theological reflection using scripture, CST, and specific Renaissance examples. Respond to: can art be a form of prayer or prophetic witness?

steps.purpose: Connect scripture and Catholic Social Teaching to the Renaissance at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.

steps.title: Closing prayer
script: Invite a student to lead a brief prayer of gratitude for the artists, writers, and musicians who insisted on the dignity of every person — and a prayer for the courage to do the same in their own lives.

screen.prayer: Creator God, you made every person in your image. Give us the courage of the Harlem Renaissance artists — to see beauty and dignity in every face, and to insist that the world see it too. Amen.

steps.purpose: Give thanks for the artists who insisted on the dignity of every person, and ask for their courage.
students: A student leads a brief prayer of gratitude — or pray the handout’s prayer together.
